568.title: Salvation came to this house (Luke 19:1–10)
568.hook: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times over
568.howItsDone: The story of Zacchaeus is read when Christians talk about repentance that changes behavior; Catholic and Orthodox teaching count making restitution as part of turning back after a wrong, and in the Roman Rite the story is read at the dedication of a church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder, and Jesus stood still to ask what he wanted. Your line was Jesus stood still.

Still in Jericho. The first half of this story is the part with the tree: a short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore to see over the crowd, and Jesus stops underneath and calls him by name. "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Today we follow them inside, because what Zacchaeus says at his own table, with the town grumbling outside, is a speech nobody asked for. Luke records no sermon from Jesus first. Zacchaeus just stands up.
screen: `TODAY I MUST ABIDE AT THY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First the grumbling. They all murmured, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Zacchaeus is a chief among the tax collectors, and rich; to the crowd, that made him a sinner. Then he stands and says, in the King James Bible: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Here's why fourfold is striking. The law of Moses had rules for paying back what you'd taken. For many wrongs, you returned it and added a fifth. But for a stolen sheep, Exodus says: "he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Zacchaeus reaches past the added fifth to the sheep thief's penalty. Nobody told him to. Jesus never mentioned money. Being welcomed did what lectures hadn't. A few scholars point out that the Greek verbs are present tense, I give, I restore, and wonder if he's describing what he already does. Others read a new promise, there and then. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." This day. Luke comes back to that word at big moments: the angels at his birth, born this day; Nazareth, this day this scripture is fulfilled; and on the cross, today again. Salvation in Luke isn't only someday. It walks into a house, sits down to dinner, and changes how the money moves.
screen: then, large: `THIS DAY IS SALVATION COME TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you owe someone, money forgotten, a favor never returned, credit that was really theirs, without spiraling into guilt. Imagine paying it back not exactly but generously, more than you owe, the way Zacchaeus did. If you pray, give thanks for being welcomed first.
Zacchaeus, the short, rich chief tax collector who climbed a tree to see Jesus, then gave half to the poor and repaid fourfold.
Your line: today, salvation. Not someday: this day, at a dinner table. See you tomorrow.

569.title: Ten pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
569.hook: Luke's version of the talents: be faithful with a little
569.howItsDone: In Christian teaching, gifts and talents are often described as given by God to be used for others, and churches encourage people to discover and use their gifts in service, in the congregation and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus, and salvation that came to a house this very day. Your line was today, salvation.

Jesus is now nigh to Jerusalem, and Luke tells us what's in the air: "they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear." Any day now. A healer and teacher heading into the capital with a crowd behind him, and people ready for a coronation. So he tells them about a coronation that takes a long time to arrive, and what to do in the meantime with very little in your hands.

A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and return. Some scholars think listeners would have recognized that: the historian Josephus tells how, after Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to have his rule confirmed, and a delegation went after him to protest. In the story, too, the citizens send word: "We will not have this man to reign over us." Before he leaves, he gives each of ten servants one pound. In Greek, a mina: a real sum, but small next to a kingdom. And here's the big difference from Matthew's parable of the talents. There, servants get different amounts. Here, everyone gets exactly the same. His instruction, in the King James Bible: "Occupy till I come." Occupy means do business, put it to work. When he returns, the first servant says: "Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds." And: "Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities." A very little. Ten cities. The reward is wildly out of proportion to the test. Another made five. Then one says: "Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin." Safe and useless, because he was afraid. The traditional reading hears the nobleman as Christ, gone away and coming back, asking what his people did with what they were given. Some modern readers notice how harsh the nobleman is and hear a warning about earthly kings instead. Either way, the question is ours: what do you do with a very little, while you wait?
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN A VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you keep wrapped up: a skill you rarely use, a little spare time, a knack for listening, cooking or fixing things. Notice what's kept it in the napkin, fear of getting it wrong or a sense it's too small to matter, and picture it put to work for someone else. If you pray, offer it back to God.
Ten pounds: ten servants, one pound each, told to put it to work until their master returns.
Your line: faithful in a very little. A very little, and ten cities. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: The stones would shout (Luke 19:28–40)
570.hook: if these were silent, the stones would cry out
570.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, many churches hold a procession with palm branches, drawing on John's Gospel, and in years when Luke is read, the reading tells of cloaks on the road and the stones that would cry out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten pounds, one each, and a servant who kept his wrapped in a napkin. Your line was faithful in a very little.

Palm Sunday. Most people picture crowds waving palm branches, children shouting hosanna. Now open Luke. No palms. No hosanna. John has the palms; Matthew and Mark have branches and hosannas. Luke's version is quieter in some ways and louder in others. He tells it from just over the Mount of Olives, on the road down into Jerusalem, and by the end even the rocks by the road are in on it.

Jesus sends two disciples for a colt, in the King James Bible "whereon yet never man sat." They throw their cloaks on it, and as he rides, people spread their clothes on the road. Cloaks, not palms. An old story in Kings has people spreading their garments under a new king's feet. And the prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humbly, riding on a colt. As the road starts down the Mount of Olives and the city comes into view, "the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen." They sing: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest." That echoes the angels at his birth: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. The angels sang it to shepherds at the start; now his followers sing it back as he comes to the city. Then some Pharisees say: "Master, rebuke thy disciples." Maybe they're worried the Romans will hear the word king. Jesus answers: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." It may echo Habakkuk, where "the stone shall cry out of the wall." There, the stones accuse injustice. Here, they'd praise. Some praise is too true to be silenced; if people won't say it, creation will.
screen: `A COLT, AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.`
then, large: `THE STONES WOULD IMMEDIATELY CRY OUT.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you've seen lately, one of Luke's mighty works, large or small: a recovery, a kindness, a sunrise, a job well done. Then say it out loud in a normal voice, even alone: thank you for this, this was good. If you pray, praise God aloud for it, and then sit in the quiet that follows.
Zechariah, the prophet who pictured Jerusalem's king coming humbly on a colt, acted out as Jesus rides down the Mount of Olives.
Your line: the stones would cry out. Some praise won't stay quiet. Day five hundred seventy, done.

571.title: He wept over the city (Luke 19:41–48)
571.hook: coming near Jerusalem, he weeps: if only you knew the things of peace
571.howItsDone: On the Mount of Olives, the small church of Dominus Flevit, Latin for the Lord wept, marks the traditional spot, and Christians around the world pray for the peace of Jerusalem and of cities in conflict, often using the words of Psalm 122.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah's humble king on a colt, and stones ready to shout. Your line was the stones would cry out.

Coming down the Mount of Olives today, the road bends, and suddenly Jerusalem is laid out across the valley: walls, domes, towers, the old city glowing gold in the late light. People stop and take photos. Luke says that when Jesus reached that point, in the middle of the singing crowd, he looked at the city. And he did something nobody around him expected on a day of celebration.

In the King James Bible: "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it." Not quiet tears. At Lazarus's tomb in John's Gospel, the word is gentler: he shed tears. Here Luke uses the word for weeping aloud, sobbing, in the middle of the parade. Then he speaks to the city as if it were a person he loves: "If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes." Tradition hears the word for peace, shalom, in Jerusalem's name. The city of peace, not knowing the things that make for peace. He describes enemies surrounding it, walls thrown down, "because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." A visitation is God coming close. Later, Roman armies did besiege Jerusalem and destroy the temple, and some Christians read these words as Jesus foreseeing it. But notice what he does with what he sees. He doesn't gloat or threaten. He weeps, the way a parent grieves a child walking toward danger. And the weeping leads to action. He goes into the temple and drives out the sellers: "My house is the house of prayer." Then he teaches there daily. The leaders want to destroy him, Luke says, but can't, because "all the people were very attentive to hear him." Tears, then a cleansing, then teaching. Love for a city does all three.
screen: then, large: `IF THOU HADST KNOWN, EVEN THOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a city where there's fighting or deep division right now, near or far, even your own town, and picture it from a hillside: the rooftops, the streets, the ordinary people inside. Let yourself feel something for them, even grief. If you pray, you can use the psalm's words, Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee, then ask in your own words for peace in the city you're picturing; if not, hold it in mind with care.
Visitation: God coming close. Weeping, Jesus says Jerusalem didn't know the time of its visitation.
Your line: if only you knew. He grieved before he did anything else. See you tomorrow.

572.title: The beloved son (Luke 20:1–19)
572.hook: the tenants kill the owner's son; the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone
572.howItsDone: Churches that follow a lectionary read the parable of the wicked tenants in their cycle of readings, and Psalm 118, with its rejected stone, is traditionally sung at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, visitation: Jesus wept over a city that didn't know its time. Your line was if only you knew.

The last week. Jesus is teaching in the temple courts every day, and the leaders come with a sharp question: by what authority do you do these things? He answers with a question about John the Baptist that they can't answer without trouble either way. So nobody answers. Then he tells the crowd a story. A man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenant farmers, and goes away a long time. At harvest he sends a servant for his share. The tenants beat him and send him back empty. A second, the same. A third, wounded and thrown out.

In the King James Bible, the owner thinks out loud: "What shall I do? I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." Three servants beaten, and he sends the person he loves most. Not a clever plan. A hopeful one, maybe a foolish one. The tenants reason the other way: this is the heir, kill him, and the vineyard is ours. They throw him out and kill him. Some in that crowd may have known the picture: in Isaiah, Israel is God's vineyard, planted with care. And beloved has been heard before in Luke: at the river, a voice from heaven called Jesus "my beloved Son." So Christians hear the story pointing at the one telling it. Luke says plainly who heard it as aimed at them: the chief priests and the scribes, who wanted to arrest him that hour and held back because they feared the people. Not a whole nation. A small circle of leaders in one tense week. Christians have sometimes forgotten that and turned this parable against Jewish people, and some churches have since said so with regret. Then Jesus quotes a psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner." The builders toss a stone aside as useless; later it holds the whole building together. The rejection isn't the end of the story. It's the turn.
screen: `A STORY AIMED AT A FEW LEADERS.`
then, large: `THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Think of something you set aside as useless: a person you wrote off at work, an idea you dropped because someone laughed, a part of yourself you keep hidden. Turn it over in your mind like a builder with a stone, more slowly than the first time, and wonder whether this is the one that holds things together. If you pray, bring it to God and leave it there.
Isaiah, the prophet whose picture of Israel as God's vineyard lies behind the parable of the owner's beloved son.
Your line: they will respect my son. Love kept on sending. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: Children of the resurrection (Luke 20:20–40)
573.hook: trick questions about taxes and the dead: for all live to him
573.howItsDone: Some churches read Jesus's answer to the Sadducees at funerals or on All Souls' Day, and some remember their dead by name in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah's vineyard, a beloved son sent last, and the stone the builders rejected. Your line was they will respect my son.

A trick question is built so every answer loses. Luke says the leaders now send spies who pretend to be sincere: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Say yes, and the crowd hears a man who bows to Rome. Say no, and Rome hears a rebel. Jesus asks whose picture is on a coin. Caesar's. Then, in the King James Bible: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's." They go quiet. Then a second group arrives with a second trap, this one about the dead.

They're Sadducees, and Luke tells us they deny any resurrection. So they spin a story to make it look ridiculous. Moses taught that if a man dies without children, his brother should marry the widow. Seven brothers, one after another, marry the same woman, and each dies. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Jesus doesn't laugh at them. He says the life to come isn't a copy of this one. People there don't marry, because they can't die any more. They are, in the King James words, "the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." That's a Hebrew way of speaking: a child of something belongs to it, and its life is shaped by it. Then Jesus goes back to Moses, to the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long after all three had died. Not the God they used to have. Their God, now. And today's line: "For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him." In this argument Jesus stands on the same side as the Pharisees, who also taught the resurrection, and some of the scribes answer, "Master, thou hast well said." After that, nobody dares ask him anything. At funerals, some Christians hear in all live to him a promise about the people they've lost: not gone from God, even when gone from us.
screen: `THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, ISAAC AND JACOB.`
then, large: `FOR ALL LIVE UNTO HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet if that's where your heart goes, and let their face or voice come near for a minute; you don't have to feel anything big. If you pray, say their name to God with Jesus' words, all live unto him. If not, hold them with gratitude and whatever hope you have.
Sadducees, the group who denied any resurrection and tried to trap Jesus with a riddle about seven brothers and one widow.
Your line: all live to him. Words to keep close on hard days. That's day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: More than all (Luke 20:41–21:4)
574.hook: beware showy religion; the widow gave out of her poverty
574.howItsDone: The phrase the widow's mite comes from the King James wording of this story, and churches read it when inviting people to give, to charity or to the church, quietly and in proportion to what they have.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sadducees' riddle, children of the resurrection, and a God of the living. Your line was all live to him.

A hospital lobby, and a donation wall: big brass plaques for the biggest gifts, a long list of names in tiny print at the bottom. In the temple courts, Jesus looks up and sees the rich putting their gifts into the treasury. Large gifts. He's just warned the crowd about religion that wants to be seen. Then a poor widow walks up and drops in two mites, tiny coins. On a plaque, her name wouldn't make the list. Jesus says something that rearranges the whole wall.

First the warning, in the King James words: "Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts." He's not attacking scribes as a group; yesterday some of them told him he'd spoken well. He's describing faith that wants an audience, and adds a harder line: they "devour widows' houses, and for a shew make long prayers." Then, straight after, a widow. Her two coins were lepta, from a Greek word meaning small, or thin. Jesus says: "Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had." The gift is measured by what's left over, and she has nothing left. Readers take this two ways, and both are in the text. The familiar reading hears praise: total trust, giving from what you'd rather keep. Some scholars notice where Luke put it, right after the warning about leaders who swallow up widows' houses, and hear a lament too: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. Either way, Jesus saw her, and Luke makes sure we do too.
screen: then, large: `ALL THE LIVING THAT SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Think of one gift no one would ever thank you for: money given quietly, an hour of help unannounced, a kind word about someone where they'll never hear it. Notice any wish to be seen giving it, without guilt, and picture giving it with no plaque and no audience. If you pray, offer it to God.
Lepta, the tiny coins a poor widow drops into the temple treasury, a gift Jesus says is more than they all gave.
Your line: out of her poverty. A week from Zacchaeus's open door to two small coins. Day five hundred seventy-four, and another week on the path.
